papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.authors: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin et al.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI, but are constrained by limited context windows, hindering their utility in tasks like extended conversations and document analysis. To enable using context beyond limited context windows, we propose virtual context management, a technique drawing inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in traditional operating systems that provide the appearance of large memory resources through data movement between fast and slow memory. Using this technique, we introduce MemGPT (Memory-GPT), a system that intelligently manages different memory tiers in order to effectively provide extended context within the LLM's limited context window, and utilizes interrupts to manage control flow between itself and the user. We evaluate our OS-inspired design in two domains where the limited context windows of modern LLMs severely handicaps their performance: document analysis, where MemGPT is able to analyze large documents that far exceed the underlying LLM's context window, and multi-session chat, where MemGPT can create conversational agents that remember, reflect, and evolve dynamically through long-term interactions with their users. We release MemGPT code and data for our experiments at https://memgpt.ai.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu et al.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across tasks in language understanding and interactive decision making, their abilities for reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought prompting) and acting (e.g. action plan generation) have primarily been studied as separate topics. In this paper, we explore the use of LLMs to generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, allowing for greater synergy between the two: reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions, while actions allow it to interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases or environments, to gather additional information. We apply our approach, named ReAct, to a diverse set of language and decision making tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines, as well as improved human interpretability and trustworthiness over methods without reasoning or acting components. Concretely, on question answering (HotpotQA) and fact verification (Fever), ReAct overcomes issues of hallucination and error propagation prevalent in chain-of-thought reasoning by interacting with a simple Wikipedia API, and generates human-like task-solving trajectories that are more interpretable than baselines without reasoning traces. On two interactive decision making benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, while being prompted with only one or two in-context examples. Project site with code: https://react-lm.github.io

papers.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
papers.authors: Timo Schick, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessì et al.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit remarkable abilities to solve new tasks from just a few examples or textual instructions, especially at scale. They also, paradoxically, struggle with basic functionality, such as arithmetic or factual lookup, where much simpler and smaller models excel. In this paper, we show that LMs can teach themselves to use external tools via simple APIs and achieve the best of both worlds. We introduce Toolformer, a model trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to best incorporate the results into future token prediction. This is done in a self-supervised way, requiring nothing more than a handful of demonstrations for each API. We incorporate a range of tools, including a calculator, a Q\&A system, two different search engines, a translation system, and a calendar. Toolformer achieves substantially improved zero-shot performance across a variety of downstream tasks, often competitive with much larger models, without sacrificing its core language modeling abilities.

papers.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao et al.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly being deployed for general problem solving across a wide range of tasks, but are still confined to token-level, left-to-right decision-making processes during inference. This means they can fall short in tasks that require exploration, strategic lookahead, or where initial decisions play a pivotal role. To surmount these challenges, we introduce a new framework for language model inference, Tree of Thoughts (ToT), which generalizes over the popular Chain of Thought approach to prompting language models, and enables exploration over coherent units of text (thoughts) that serve as intermediate steps toward problem solving. ToT allows LMs to perform deliberate decision making by considering multiple different reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to decide the next course of action, as well as looking ahead or backtracking when necessary to make global choices. Our experiments show that ToT significantly enhances language models' problem-solving abilities on three novel tasks requiring non-trivial planning or search: Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords. For instance, in Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%. Code repo with all prompts: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm.

papers.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
papers.authors: Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang et al.
papers.abstract: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large language models (LLMs) often produce responses containing factual inaccuracies due to their sole reliance on the parametric knowledge they encapsulate. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), an ad hoc approach that augments LMs with retrieval of relevant knowledge, decreases such issues. However, indiscriminately retrieving and incorporating a fixed number of retrieved passages, regardless of whether retrieval is necessary, or passages are relevant, diminishes LM versatility or can lead to unhelpful response generation. We introduce a new framework called Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) that enhances an LM's quality and factuality through retrieval and self-reflection. Our framework trains a single arbitrary LM that adaptively retrieves passages on-demand, and generates and reflects on retrieved passages and its own generations using special tokens, called reflection tokens. Generating reflection tokens makes the LM controllable during the inference phase, enabling it to tailor its behavior to diverse task requirements. Experiments show that Self-RAG (7B and 13B parameters) significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLMs and retrieval-augmented models on a diverse set of tasks. Specifically, Self-RAG outperforms ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on Open-domain QA, reasoning and fact verification tasks, and it shows significant gains in improving factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generations relative to these models.

papers.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman et al.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly used to interact with external environments (e.g., games, compilers, APIs) as goal-driven agents. However, it remains challenging for these language agents to quickly and efficiently learn from trial-and-error as traditional reinforcement learning methods require extensive training samples and expensive model fine-tuning. We propose Reflexion, a novel framework to reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback. Concretely, Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals, then maintain their own reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials. Reflexion is flexible enough to incorporate various types (scalar values or free-form language) and sources (external or internally simulated) of feedback signals, and obtains significant improvements over a baseline agent across diverse tasks (sequential decision-making, coding, language reasoning). For example, Reflexion achieves a 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4 that achieves 80%. We also conduct ablation and analysis studies using different feedback signals, feedback incorporation methods, and agent types, and provide insights into how they affect performance.

papers.title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Shi-Qi Yan, Jia-Chen Gu, Yun Zhu et al.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) inevitably exhibit hallucinations since the accuracy of generated texts cannot be secured solely by the parametric knowledge they encapsulate. Although retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a practicable complement to LLMs, it relies heavily on the relevance of retrieved documents, raising concerns about how the model behaves if retrieval goes wrong. To this end, we propose the Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG) to improve the robustness of generation. Specifically, a lightweight retrieval evaluator is designed to assess the overall quality of retrieved documents for a query, returning a confidence degree based on which different knowledge retrieval actions can be triggered. Since retrieval from static and limited corpora can only return sub-optimal documents, large-scale web searches are utilized as an extension for augmenting the retrieval results. Besides, a decompose-then-recompose algorithm is designed for retrieved documents to selectively focus on key information and filter out irrelevant information in them. CRAG is plug-and-play and can be seamlessly coupled with various RAG-based approaches. Experiments on four datasets covering short- and long-form generation tasks show that CRAG can significantly improve the performance of RAG-based approaches.

papers.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
papers.authors: Lei Wang, Wanyu Xu, Yihuai Lan et al.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been shown to deliver impressive performance in various NLP tasks. To tackle multi-step reasoning tasks, few-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting includes a few manually crafted step-by-step reasoning demonstrations which enable LLMs to explicitly generate reasoning steps and improve their reasoning task accuracy. To eliminate the manual effort, Zero-shot-CoT concatenates the target problem statement with "Let's think step by step" as an input prompt to LLMs. Despite the success of Zero-shot-CoT, it still suffers from three pitfalls: calculation errors, missing-step errors, and semantic misunderstanding errors. To address the missing-step errors, we propose Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting. It consists of two components: first, devising a plan to divide the entire task into smaller subtasks, and then carrying out the subtasks according to the plan. To address the calculation errors and improve the quality of generated reasoning steps, we extend PS prompting with more detailed instructions and derive PS+ prompting. We evaluate our proposed prompting strategy on ten datasets across three reasoning problems. The experimental results over GPT-3 show that our proposed zero-shot prompting consistently outperforms Zero-shot-CoT across all datasets by a large margin, is comparable to or exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought Prompting, and has comparable performance with 8-shot CoT prompting on the math reasoning problem. The code can be found at https://github.com/AGI-Edgerunners/Plan-and-Solve-Prompting.

research_gaps.title: No Unified Integration of Memory, Reasoning, and Tool Use
research_gaps.description: The collection treats memory management (MemGPT, Reflexion), deliberate reasoning (ToT, Plan-and-Solve, ReAct), and tool use (Toolformer) as largely separate capabilities, with no paper proposing a unified architecture that jointly manages persistent memory, multi-step planning, and external tool invocation. This matters because real-world agentic tasks typically require all three simultaneously, and their interactions (e.g., how memory state should inform tool selection, or how tool outputs should be stored and retrieved) remain unstudied.

section_drafts.content:
The Introduction section covers research on enhancing LLM capabilities through memory and context management (MemGPT, Reflexion), reasoning and planning strategies (ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, Plan-and-Solve prompting), and tool use with external API integration (Toolformer). It also addresses retrieval-augmented generation combined with self-critique mechanisms (Self-RAG, Corrective RAG), collectively framing efforts to make language models more autonomous, adaptive, and reliable.

## Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly evolved from passive text generators into the core reasoning engine of autonomous agents capable of planning, acting, and interacting with external environments. This transition has been driven by a growing body of work that augments LLMs with mechanisms for structured reasoning, dynamic memory management, external tool invocation, and retrieval-augmented generation. Together, these capabilities form the foundation of what is increasingly referred to as LLM agent reasoning, tool use, and retrieval—a research area concerned with enabling models to solve complex, multi-step tasks that exceed the scope of a single forward pass. This review synthesizes the current literature across four interconnected clusters: memory and context management, reasoning and planning strategies, tool use and external API integration, and retrieval-augmented generation with self-critique. In doing so, it identifies the methodological evolution of the field, compares competing design philosophies, and highlights critical gaps that remain unaddressed.

The earliest strand of agentic LLM research focused on overcoming the fundamental constraint of limited context windows. MemGPT proposed a virtual context management system inspired by hierarchical memory in operating systems, moving data between fast and slow memory tiers to provide extended context within the model's fixed window [1]. In parallel, Reflexion introduced a complementary form of persistence: rather than managing raw context, it reinforced language agents through verbal self-reflection stored in an episodic memory buffer, enabling trial-and-error learning without weight updates [2]. These two approaches illustrate a key divergence in the memory literature—MemGPT treats memory as an architectural resource management problem, whereas Reflexion treats it as a learning signal for behavioral improvement. Both, however, share the assumption that memory is a separable capability, an assumption that later work would implicitly challenge.

A second major strand concerns reasoning and planning. ReAct established a foundational paradigm by prompting LLMs to generate interleaved reasoning traces and task-specific actions, demonstrating that the synergy between "thinking" and "acting" improves performance and interpretability across diverse language and decision-making tasks [3]. Tree of Thoughts (ToT) extended this line by generalizing chain-of-thought prompting into a search over coherent text units, allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate intermediate choices, and look ahead or backtrack [4]. Plan-and-Solve prompting took a different tack, addressing missing-step errors in zero-shot chain-of-thought by instructing models to first devise a plan and then execute sub-tasks sequentially [5]. The evolution here is instructive: early work (ReAct) treated reasoning as a linear interleaving of thought and action, whereas ToT introduced branching search and Plan-and-Solve introduced explicit decomposition—each representing progressively more structured and deliberate forms of problem solving.

Tool use represents a third distinct capability. Toolformer demonstrated that language models can teach themselves to call external APIs in a self-supervised manner, learning to decide which APIs to invoke, when, with what arguments, and how to incorporate results into subsequent token prediction [6]. This work is notable for framing tool use as a learned behavior rather than a hand-engineered pipeline, and for showing that such learning can improve zero-shot performance without sacrificing core language modeling ability. Compared to the reasoning literature, which largely relies on prompting strategies at inference time, Toolformer represents a more training-centric approach—a contrast that recurs throughout the field.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and self-critique form the fourth cluster. Self-RAG trains a model to adaptively retrieve passages on demand and to generate self-reflection tokens that critique retrieval relevance, support, and utility, addressing the problem that indiscriminate retrieval can diminish versatility or produce unhelpful responses [7]. Corrective RAG (CRAG) takes a complementary approach, employing a lightweight retrieval evaluator to assess document quality and trigger corrective actions such as large-scale web searches when confidence is low [8]. Both works reflect a broader shift from static, always-on retrieval toward adaptive, quality-aware retrieval—yet they differ in mechanism: Self-RAG internalizes critique into the model's generation process, while CRAG externalizes it into a separate evaluator module.

Across these four clusters, several comparative observations emerge. First, there is a clear methodological tension between inference-time strategies (ReAct, ToT, Plan-and-Solve, Reflexion) and training-time approaches (Toolformer, Self-RAG). The former offer flexibility and require no fine-tuning, while the latter promise more deeply integrated capabilities at the cost of training infrastructure. Second, the clusters have developed largely in isolation: memory management, reasoning, tool use, and retrieval are each treated as separable problems, and no paper in this collection proposes a unified architecture that jointly manages persistent memory, multi-step planning, and external tool invocation [Gap 1]. This is a significant limitation, since real-world agentic tasks typically require all three simultaneously, and the interactions among them—such as how memory state should inform tool selection, or how tool outputs should be stored and retrieved—remain unstudied.

A further gap concerns evaluation. Each method is assessed on its own task suite—ToT on puzzle tasks, Toolformer on API-calling datasets, Self-RAG and CRAG on question-answering benchmarks—with no shared benchmark enabling head-to-head comparison across memory, reasoning, retrieval, and tool-use approaches [Gap 2]. Consequently, it is impossible to determine which technique, or combination of techniques, yields the best cost/accuracy trade-off for general agentic workloads. This problem is compounded by the underexplored cost and latency of deliberate reasoning: methods such as ToT, Reflexion, and Self-RAG add substantial inference-time computation through branching search, iterative self-reflection, and multiple retrieval/critique passes, yet none of the papers quantify or optimize compute and latency relative to accuracy gains [Gap 3]. As these techniques move toward deployment, the absence of cost-aware evaluation and budgeted-reasoning methods becomes increasingly consequential.

Two additional gaps merit attention. First, no mechanism is proposed for reconciling conflicting retrieved or remembered information: retrieval and memory papers focus on whether to retrieve or how to store context, but none address what happens when retrieved documents, stored memories, or tool outputs contradict one another [Gap 4]. Provenance tracking, confidence weighting, and consistency checking are essential for trustworthy long-horizon agents but are absent from the collection. Second, the self-critique mechanisms central to Self-RAG, CRAG, and Reflexion are assumed to be reliable, yet none of the papers examine when self-critique fails—through systematic blind spots, sycophantic self-evaluation, or error compounding across reflection iterations [Gap 6]. Finally, the predominance of short, synthetic, or single-turn benchmarks leaves long-horizon, multi-session, real-world agentic tasks largely untested, meaning that claims about memory persistence, iterative self-improvement, and planning are not validated under realistic deployment conditions [Gap 5].

In summary, the literature on LLM agent reasoning, tool use, and retrieval has produced a rich set of techniques spanning memory architectures, deliberate reasoning strategies, self-supervised tool learning, and adaptive retrieval with self-critique. These methods have advanced the field from simple prompting to increasingly structured and autonomous agentic behavior. However, the field remains fragmented: capabilities are developed and evaluated in isolation, cost and latency trade-offs are unquantified, conflict resolution and self-critique failure modes are unaddressed, and realistic long-horizon evaluation is scarce. These gaps motivate the unified, cost-aware, and robustness-oriented research directions that the remainder of this review examines.

### Method Comparison

# Comparative Analysis of Introduction-Section Approaches

## Overview Table

| Paper | Core Mechanism | Learning Signal | Memory/State | Control Flow |
|-------|---------------|-----------------|--------------|--------------|
| **MemGPT** | OS-inspired hierarchical memory | Prompting (no training) | Tiered (fast/slow) + interrupts | System-managed via interrupts |
| **ReAct** | Interleaved reasoning + acting | Prompting (few-shot) | Reasoning trace (in-context) | Model-driven interleaving |
| **Toolformer** | Self-supervised API calling | Self-supervised (few examples) | None explicit | Model decides when/what to call |
| **Tree of Thoughts** | Search over thought tree | Prompting + self-evaluation | Explicit tree of thoughts | Deliberate search (BFS/DFS) |
| **Self-RAG** | Adaptive retrieval + self-critique tokens | Trained (reflection tokens) | Reflection token stream | Model-driven, token-gated |
| **Reflexion** | Verbal reflection + episodic memory | Verbal RL (no weight updates) | Episodic memory buffer | Trial-based, feedback-driven |
| **Corrective RAG** | Retrieval quality evaluator | Lightweight evaluator (trained) | Confidence signal | Conditional retrieval actions |
| **Plan-and-Solve** | Plan-then-execute prompting | Prompting (zero-shot) | Plan as text | Two-stage (plan → execute) |

---

## Key Similarities

**1. Augmenting LLMs with external structure.** All eight papers address a shared limitation: vanilla LLMs lack mechanisms for memory, verification, tool use, or structured deliberation. Each introduces an auxiliary structure—memory tiers (MemGPT), action spaces (ReAct, Toolformer), search trees (ToT), reflection tokens (Self-RAG), memory buffers (Reflexion), evaluators (CRAG), or explicit plans (PS).

**2. Decomposition of the reasoning/acting loop.** ReAct, ToT, PS, and Reflexion all break problem-solving into discrete, inspectable steps (thoughts, plans, reflections) rather than monolithic generation. MemGPT and Self-RAG similarly decompose generation into managed sub-operations (memory reads/writes, retrieval critiques).

**3. Self-evaluation as a control signal.** ToT (self-evaluating choices), Self-RAG (support/utility critiques), Reflexion (feedback-driven reflection), and CRAG (confidence degree) all introduce a self-assessment step that gates subsequent behavior—a shared "generate-then-judge" pattern.

**4. Minimal supervision.** Toolformer (few examples), Self-RAG (trained but self-generated labels), CRAG (lightweight evaluator), and the prompting-based methods (ReAct, ToT, PS, Reflexion, MemGPT) all emphasize reducing reliance on heavy human annotation.

---

## Key Differences

**1. Training vs. prompting.**
- **Trained/prompted hybrids:** Toolformer, Self-RAG, and CRAG train components (API-call prediction, reflection tokens, retrieval evaluator).
- **Pure prompting:** ReAct, ToT, PS, Reflexion, and MemGPT require no weight updates—they operate entirely through prompting and external scaffolding.
- This is the sharpest divide: *parametric* adaptation (Toolformer, Self-RAG) vs. *non-parametric* orchestration (MemGPT, Reflexion).

**2. Nature of the external state.**
- **Persistent memory:** MemGPT (tiered OS-like memory), Reflexion (episodic buffer across trials).
- **Transient structure:** ToT (tree within a single problem), ReAct (in-context trace), PS (plan text).
- **No explicit state:** Toolformer, Self-RAG, CRAG operate per-step without a persistent store.

**3. Control-flow philosophy.**
- **Interrupt/OS-driven:** MemGPT uniquely borrows *interrupts* and data movement from operating systems—control flow is system-managed.
- **Search-driven:** ToT explicitly frames solving as tree search with lookahead/backtracking—the most deliberate, compute-heavy control structure.
- **Reactive/conditional:** CRAG triggers different retrieval actions based on a confidence score; Self-RAG gates retrieval via tokens.
- **Sequential/trial-based:** Reflexion iterates across trials; PS is a fixed two-stage plan-then-execute.

**4. Role of retrieval/external knowledge.**
- **Central:** Self-RAG (adaptive retrieval + critique), CRAG (retrieval quality assessment + web search fallback).
- **Absent:** ToT, PS, Reflexion, MemGPT focus on reasoning/memory rather than retrieval.
- **Tool-as-API:** Toolformer treats external calls (including search) as learnable API invocations.

**5. Granularity of the unit of operation.**
-

### Strengths

# Key Strengths and Advantages of the Described Methods

**1. Hierarchical memory management enabling unbounded context (MemGPT).** MemGPT borrows the OS principle of tiered memory—moving data between fast (in-context) and slow (external) storage—so an LLM can maintain coherent long-term state beyond its fixed context window. The use of interrupts to manage control flow between the system and the LLM gives fine-grained, event-driven control over when memory operations occur, making the approach scalable to extended conversations and documents.

**2. Interleaved reasoning and acting for grounded, adaptive task execution (ReAct).** By generating reasoning traces alongside task-specific actions, ReAct lets the model induce, track, and update action plans while handling exceptions as they arise. This synergy between deliberation and environment interaction improves both interpretability and robustness compared to reasoning-only or acting-only baselines, since actions supply external feedback that corrects faulty reasoning.

**3. Self-supervised tool learning without heavy annotation (Toolformer).** Toolformer trains a model to decide *which* APIs to call, *when*, with *what arguments*, and *how* to incorporate results into future token prediction—using only a handful of demonstrations per API. This self-supervised formulation makes tool use learnable at scale without expensive human-labeled trajectories, and the learned decisions are made inline during generation.

**4. Deliberate search over reasoning paths with self-evaluation (Tree of Thoughts).** ToT frames problem solving as search over a tree of coherent "thought" units, allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate intermediate choices, and look ahead or backtrack. This explicit search structure substantially improves performance on problems requiring planning and exploration, where single-pass chain-of-thought fails.

**5. Self-critique and verbal reflection for continual improvement (Self-RAG, Reflexion, Corrective RAG).** Self-RAG trains the LM to adaptively retrieve on demand and emit self-reflection tokens (retrieval, relevance, support, utility) that assess and improve its own output; Reflexion stores verbal reflections on feedback in episodic memory to induce better decisions in later trials; Corrective RAG uses a lightweight retrieval evaluator whose confidence score triggers different retrieval actions (including large-scale web search). Together these show that models can monitor, critique, and correct their own generation and retrieval without retraining the base model.

**6. Structured planning before execution (Plan-and-Solve).** PS prompting replaces the generic "Let's think step by step" with explicit instructions to understand the problem, extract variables, and devise a plan before executing it step by step (with PS+ adding further refinement). This decomposition reduces missing-step and calculation errors in zero-shot reasoning, improving reliability without task-specific exemplars.

### Limitations

# Key Limitations and Weaknesses Across the Papers

**1. Heavy reliance on LLM self-evaluation without external grounding (Self-RAG, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts).**
Self-RAG, Reflexion, and ToT all depend on the model's own judgments—self-reflection tokens, verbal self-critiques, or self-evaluated thought states—to guide retrieval, memory updates, or search. These signals inherit the model's biases and calibration errors; a model that cannot reliably judge correctness will propagate flawed critiques. Reflexion's episodic memory can also reinforce incorrect reflections across trials, and ToT's self-evaluation of intermediate thoughts is only as good as the base model's discrimination ability.

**2. Fixed or coarse-grained control policies that limit adaptivity (MemGPT, Corrective RAG, Toolformer).**
MemGPT's OS-inspired memory hierarchy relies on predefined paging/interrupt rules rather than learned policies, so memory management is heuristic and may not suit all task distributions. Corrective RAG uses a lightweight evaluator returning a confidence degree that triggers a small set of discrete actions (correct/incorrect/ambiguous), which is coarse and threshold-sensitive. Toolformer decides API calls via a perplexity-based self-supervised filter with a fixed threshold, which can miss useful calls or admit spurious ones and does not model multi-step tool composition.

**3. Cost, latency, and token overhead from iterative deliberation (Tree of Thoughts, ReAct, Plan-and-Solve).**
ToT requires branching, self-evaluation, and lookahead at each node, multiplying inference cost and latency relative to single-pass generation. ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions, increasing token usage and environment interactions per task. Plan-and-Solve adds an explicit planning stage before execution, adding overhead and—because the plan is fixed before execution—risking brittle plans that are not revised when intermediate steps fail.

**4. Weak guarantees on plan execution, error recovery, and grounding (ReAct, Plan-and-Solve, MemGPT).**
ReAct's reasoning traces are unverified natural language and can hallucinate actions or loop; exception handling is ad hoc. Plan-and-Solve commits to a plan up front and executes step by step without a built-in mechanism to detect or repair plan failures. MemGPT's interrupt-driven control flow assumes the system can reliably detect when to yield control, but mis-triggered or missed interrupts can cause context loss or redundant memory operations.

**5. Dependence on curated supervision/feedback signals and limited generalization evidence (Toolformer, Reflexion, Self-RAG).**
Toolformer requires a hand-designed set of APIs and self-supervised filtering to build training data, so it does not generalize to arbitrary tools or compositional multi-tool use. Reflexion depends on task feedback signals (e.g., success/failure or scalar rewards) that may be sparse, noisy, or unavailable in open-ended settings. Self-RAG requires training with reflection tokens and retrieval annotations, and its benefits are tied to the retrieval corpus and training distribution, with limited evidence of robustness to distribution shift.

The Related Work section covers four key research areas: memory and context management for LLMs (including operating-system-inspired architectures and verbal reinforcement learning for agents), reasoning and planning strategies (such as interleaved reasoning-acting, deliberate tree-based problem solving, and zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting), tool use and external API integration (enabling models to teach themselves to invoke tools), and retrieval-augmented generation with self-critique (incorporating self-reflection and corrective retrieval mechanisms).

## Related Work

Research on large language model (LLM) agents has progressed along several largely parallel strands: managing limited context through hierarchical memory, eliciting deliberate multi-step reasoning, extending model capabilities through external tools, and grounding generation in retrieved evidence. This section organizes prior work into these categories, compares their underlying mechanisms, and identifies the open problems that motivate the present study.

### Memory and Context Management

A first line of work addresses the fundamental constraint of fixed context windows. MemGPT draws on the design of operating systems, proposing virtual context management in which data is moved between fast and slow memory tiers and control flow is coordinated through interrupts, thereby providing extended effective context within the model's window [1]. Reflexion takes a complementary approach at the level of learning: rather than managing what is stored, it reinforces agents through linguistic feedback, having them verbally reflect on task signals and persist reflective text in an episodic memory buffer that informs subsequent trials, thus achieving trial-and-error improvement without weight updates [2]. Together, these systems establish two distinct roles for memory—as a managed substrate for context [1] and as a repository of accumulated self-knowledge [2]—but neither examines how memory contents should interact with reasoning or tool selection.

### Reasoning and Planning Strategies

A second cluster concerns how LLMs structure their own problem solving. ReAct established the influential pattern of interleaving reasoning traces with task-specific actions, allowing reasoning to induce and update action plans while actions ground subsequent reasoning in external observations [3]. Tree of Thoughts generalizes chain-of-thought prompting from a left-to-right token-level process to a search over a tree of coherent "thought" units, enabling the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate intermediate choices, and look ahead or backtrack [4]. Plan-and-Solve prompting targets the missing-step errors of zero-shot chain-of-thought by first instructing the model to devise a plan—understanding the problem and extracting variables—and then executing sub-tasks step by step [5]. The evolution here is instructive: early prompting elicited linear reasoning, ReAct coupled that reasoning to acting [3], and subsequent methods added explicit search [4] or explicit decomposition [5]. Yet these strategies remain primarily inference-time prompting schemes, and none is integrated with persistent memory or systematic tool invocation.

### Tool Use and External API Integration

Toolformer demonstrated that models can acquire tool-use competence self-supervisedly, learning to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to incorporate results into future token prediction, achieving improved zero-shot performance without sacrificing core language modeling abilities [6]. This work is notable for internalizing tool use into the model itself, in contrast to prompting-based approaches such as ReAct that elicit actions at inference time [3]. However, Toolformer treats tool calls as largely local decisions within a generation, leaving open how tool use should be sequenced within long-horizon plans or informed by stored memory.

### Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Self-Critique

A fourth strand improves factuality by grounding generation in retrieved evidence while making retrieval itself adaptive. Self-RAG trains a model to retrieve passages on demand and to emit self-reflection tokens—retrieval, relevance, support, and utility critiques—that assess and improve its own generation, motivated by the observation that indiscriminate retrieval can diminish versatility or yield unhelpful responses [7]. Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG) instead places a lightweight retrieval evaluator upstream, assigning a confidence degree to retrieved documents and triggering different knowledge retrieval actions, including large-scale web searches, when quality is judged insufficient [8]. Both approaches embody a shift from static retrieve-then-generate pipelines toward self-assessing, corrective loops [7, 8], paralleling the reflective mechanisms seen in agent memory work [2].

### Comparison and Open Problems

Across these clusters, a clear trajectory emerges: from static prompting toward adaptive, self-evaluating loops that decide when to reason further [4], when to act or call a tool [3, 6], when to retrieve [7, 8], and what to remember [1, 2]. Despite this shared direction, the literature exhibits several gaps. First, the clusters remain largely disjoint: memory management [1, 2], deliberate reasoning [3–5], and tool use [6] are studied as separate capabilities, and no architecture jointly manages persistent memory, multi-step planning, and external tool invocation—despite real-world agentic tasks typically requiring all three, with their interactions (e.g., how memory state should inform tool selection) left unstudied. Second, evaluation is fragmented: each method is assessed on its own task suite—puzzle tasks for tree search [4], API-calling datasets for tool learning [6], and question answering for retrieval methods [7, 8]—so no shared benchmark permits head-to-head comparison of memory, reasoning, retrieval, and tool

# Comparison of Methods Across Papers (Related Work Section)

## Overview of Each Approach

| Paper | Core Mechanism | Key Innovation |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **MemGPT** | OS-inspired hierarchical memory with data movement between fast/slow tiers; interrupts manage control flow | Virtual context management via memory paging |
| **ReAct** | Interleaved reasoning traces + task-specific actions in a prompting loop | Synergy of reasoning and acting |
| **Toolformer** | Self-supervised learning to decide which APIs to call, when, with what arguments, and how to use results | Self-taught tool use without human annotation |
| **Tree of Thoughts (ToT)** | Search over a tree of "thought" nodes with self-evaluation and lookahead/backtracking | Deliberate multi-path problem solving |
| **Self-RAG** | Adaptive on-demand retrieval + self-reflection tokens (retrieval, relevance, support, utility) | Self-critical retrieval-augmented generation |
| **Reflexion** | Verbal reflection on feedback stored in episodic memory to improve later trials | Verbal reinforcement learning without weight updates |
| **Corrective RAG (CRAG)** | Lightweight retrieval evaluator returns confidence → triggers different retrieval actions (incl. web search) | Confidence-driven corrective retrieval |
| **Plan-and-Solve (PS/PS+)** | Prompt instructs LLM to understand problem, extract variables, plan, then execute step by step | Structured zero-shot planning replacing "step by step" |

---

## Similarities (Grouped by Theme)

### 1. Iterative / Multi-step Reasoning Loops
- **ReAct, ToT, Reflexion, Self-RAG, PS+** all decompose problem solving into multiple stages rather than a single forward pass.
- **ReAct** interleaves thought→action→observation; **ToT** expands/ evaluates/prunes tree nodes; **Reflexion** iterates across trials; **PS+** plans then executes step by step.

### 2. Self-Evaluation / Self-Critique
- **ToT** self-evaluates candidate thoughts; **Self-RAG** emits critique tokens (relevance, support, utility); **Reflexion** verbally reflects on feedback; **CRAG** uses an evaluator to score retrieved documents.
- Common thread: the model (or a lightweight module) judges its own intermediate output to steer next steps.

### 3. External Information / Tool Grounding
- **ReAct** calls tools/APIs; **Toolformer** learns API calls; **Self-RAG** and **CRAG** retrieve external passages (CRAG can escalate to web search); **MemGPT** moves data across memory tiers.
- All address the limitation of static parametric knowledge by incorporating external signals.

### 4. Memory / State Management
- **MemGPT** (hierarchical tiers), **Reflexion** (episodic buffer), **ToT** (tree frontier), **ReAct** (trajectory context) all maintain structured state beyond a single prompt.

### 5. Prompting vs. Training Spectrum
- **PS, ReAct, ToT, Reflexion** are largely **prompting/inference-time** techniques (no weight updates).
- **Toolformer, Self-RAG** involve **training/fine-tuning** the model to internalize the behavior.
- **MemGPT, CRAG** combine system-level orchestration with (lightweight) components.

---

## Key Differences

### A. Locus of Control
- **MemGPT**: OS-level control — interrupts and memory paging govern *when* the system acts.
- **ReAct / Reflexion / ToT**: Model-level control — the LLM decides next thought/action.
- **Toolformer**: Learned policy baked into weights (implicit control).
- **CRAG**: External evaluator gates retrieval actions (modular control).

### B. Nature of the "Memory"
- **MemGPT**: Explicit tiered memory (fast/slow), analogous to RAM/disk.
- **Reflexion**: Episodic buffer of *verbal* reflections (qualitative, linguistic).
- **ToT**: Transient tree structure (search frontier), not persistent memory.
- **ReAct**: Working context (trajectory), not a managed store.

### C. Search Strategy
- **ToT**: Explicit tree search with lookahead and backtracking (deliberate exploration).
- **ReAct**: Greedy linear interleaving (no backtracking).
- **PS/PS+**: Single planned decomposition (no branching).
- **Reflexion**: Trial-and-error across episodes (implicit search over attempts).

### D. Retrieval Handling
- **Self-RAG**: Model *decides* when to retrieve and critiques retrieved content via learned tokens.
- **CRAG**: Separate evaluator assigns confidence and triggers *corrective* actions (including web search).
- **ReAct**: Retrie

# Key Strengths and Advantages of the Described Methods

**1. Hierarchical memory management enabling unbounded context (MemGPT)**
MemGPT's OS-inspired design—moving data between fast and slow memory tiers and using interrupts to manage control flow—lets LLMs operate over effectively unbounded context while keeping the active working set small. This decouples model capability from fixed context-window limits, a structural advantage over flat-context approaches.

**2. Grounded, adaptive reasoning through interleaved thought and action (ReAct; Tree of Thoughts)**
ReAct's interleaved reasoning traces and task-specific actions let the model induce, track, and update plans and handle exceptions as they arise, grounding reasoning in external feedback rather than pure introspection. Tree of Thoughts extends this by framing problem solving as search over a tree of coherent "thought" units, enabling deliberate exploration of multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluation of choices, and lookahead/backtracking—advantages neither single-pass CoT nor pure acting provides.

**3. Self-supervised tool acquisition and adaptive retrieval (Toolformer; Self-RAG)**
Toolformer shows an LM can learn *which* APIs to call, *when*, *with what arguments*, and *how to incorporate results*—all via self-supervised learning from only a handful of demonstrations per API, avoiding costly human annotation. Self-RAG similarly trains the model to retrieve passages *on demand* and emit self-reflection tokens (retrieval, relevance, support, utility critiques), making retrieval adaptive rather than always-on and giving the model a mechanism to assess and improve its own generations.

**4. Closed-loop self-correction via verbal reinforcement and retrieval critique (Reflexion; Corrective RAG)**
Reflexion lets agents verbally reflect on task feedback and store reflections in an episodic memory buffer, inducing better decisions in subsequent trials without weight updates—an efficient alternative to gradient-based RL. Corrective RAG adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator that returns a confidence degree triggering different retrieval actions (including large-scale web search), improving robustness when initial retrieval is poor.

**5. Structured zero-shot planning that reduces reasoning errors (Plan-and-Solve Prompting)**
PS prompting replaces the generic "Let's think step by step" with explicit instructions to understand the problem, extract variables, and create a plan before executing it step by step (with PS+ adding further refinement). This decomposition targets missing-calculation and missing-step errors common in zero-shot CoT, improving reliability without task-specific exemplars.

**Cross-cutting advantage:** Together these methods shift LLMs from single-pass generators into systems with *memory* (MemGPT, Reflexion), *deliberation* (ToT, ReAct), *self-assessment* (Self-RAG, CRAG), and *tool/plan structure* (Toolformer, PS)—each addressing a distinct failure mode of naive prompting while remaining largely training-light or self-supervised.

# Key Limitations and Weaknesses Across the Papers

**1. Heavy reliance on the base LLM's self-evaluation, which is unreliable and can compound errors.**
Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) depends on the model self-evaluating intermediate "thoughts" to prune/search the tree, but LLM self-assessment is often miscalibrated, so a bad evaluator corrupts the search. Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023) similarly trains the model to emit its own critique tokens (relevance, support, utility), which inherits the model's biases and can produce overconfident or sycophantic self-critiques. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) relies on the agent correctly interpreting sparse feedback signals to generate useful verbal reflections—weak or ambiguous feedback yields shallow, misleading lessons stored in memory.

**2. Brittle, hand-designed control mechanisms and thresholds.**
Corrective RAG (Yan et al., 2024) hinges on a lightweight retrieval evaluator returning a confidence score that triggers discrete actions (correct/incorrect/ambiguous), making performance sensitive to threshold tuning and to the evaluator's calibration. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) depends on the LLM correctly issuing memory-management function calls and interrupts; failures in function-calling or poor paging decisions degrade the hierarchical memory system, and the OS analogy imposes engineering overhead without guaranteeing correct data movement.

**3. Limited generalization beyond the training/self-supervised distribution and tool/API coverage.**
Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) learns API calls via self-supervision on a handful of tools, so it does not generalize to unseen APIs and its utility filter can discard useful calls or retain spurious ones; it also optimizes token-level likelihood rather than task success. Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al., 2023) is a prompting scheme with no learning, so gains are inconsistent across task types and it can produce plans that are plausible but not executable, with no mechanism to verify or repair the plan.

**4. Lack of grounded verification and vulnerability to hallucinated reasoning/actions.**
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves reasoning and actions but has no guarantee that reasoning traces are faithful or that actions are correct; errors propagate across steps and the loop can stall or loop indefinitely without a robust failure-recovery mechanism. Self-RAG and Corrective RAG mitigate but do not eliminate hallucination—retrieval critiques can be wrong, and web-search fallbacks (CRAG) introduce noisy or irrelevant evidence.

**5. Scalability, cost, and memory/state-management overhead.**
Tree of Thoughts multiplies inference cost through branching and look-ahead, making it impractical for large search spaces or latency-sensitive settings. MemGPT's tiered memory and interrupt-driven control add complexity and token overhead for paging, and its effectiveness depends on the LLM's ability to manage its own context—an ability that degrades as memory grows. Reflexion's episodic buffer grows unbounded and can accumulate stale or contradictory reflections that mislead later trials.

**6. Evaluation narrowness / task-specific design.**
Most methods are validated on narrow benchmarks (e.g., ToT on puzzles like Game of 24 and crosswords; Toolformer on a fixed tool set; Reflexion on specific agent tasks), limiting evidence of robustness in open-ended, real-world deployment where feedback is sparse and tools/APIs are heterogeneous.

The "Methods and Approaches" section covers four key research topics: memory and context management for LLMs (MemGPT, Reflexion), reasoning and planning strategies (ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, Plan-and-Solve prompting), tool use and external API integration (Toolformer), and retrieval-augmented generation with self-critique (Self-RAG, Corrective RAG). These clusters collectively address how language agents manage context, deliberate through multi-step problems, leverage external tools, and self-reflect to improve retrieval and generation quality.

## Methods and Approaches

Research on LLM agent reasoning, tool use, and retrieval has converged on a set of complementary strategies for extending the capabilities of frozen language models beyond single-pass generation. Across the reviewed literature, methods can be organized into four broad categories: (i) reasoning and planning strategies that structure the model's internal deliberation, (ii) memory and context management mechanisms that extend effective context beyond the model's window, (iii) tool use and external API integration, and (iv) retrieval-augmented generation coupled with self-critique. While each category addresses a distinct limitation, the approaches share a common underlying premise: that agentic competence can be elicited through inference-time scaffolding rather than weight updates, and they differ primarily in where that scaffolding is applied—to the reasoning trace, the memory hierarchy, the action space, or the knowledge source.

**Reasoning and planning strategies.** Plan-and-Solve prompting addresses missing-step errors in zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning by guiding LLMs to first devise a plan and then execute sub-tasks; its prompt instructs the model to understand the problem, extract variables, and create a plan, then carry out the plan step by step, improving zero-shot multi-step reasoning accuracy [1]. ReAct explores using LLMs to generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, enabling synergy between reasoning and acting; its prompting approach has the model generate interleaved reasoning traces and task-specific actions, where reasoning traces help induce, track, and update action plans and handle exceptions while actions interface with external environments, and the paper demonstrates effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines on diverse language and decision-making tasks with improved human interpretability [2]. Tree of Thoughts (ToT) generalizes chain-of-thought prompting to enable deliberate problem solving by exploring multiple reasoning paths over coherent text units ("thoughts"), framing problem solving as search over a tree where nodes are coherent units of text, allowing the model to consider multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate choices, and look ahead or backtrack—addressing the limitation of token-level left-to-right decision-making on tasks requiring exploration [3]. Taken together, this line of work traces an evolution from structured plan-then-execute prompting [1] to interleaved reasoning-acting loops [2] to explicit search over reasoning states [3], with each step trading additional inference-time computation for greater deliberative control.

**Memory and context management.** A parallel strand addresses the fixed context window as a bottleneck for long-horizon agency. MemGPT draws inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in operating systems, proposing virtual context management in which data is moved between fast and slow memory tiers and interrupts manage control flow between the system and the model, thereby providing extended context within the LLM's limited context window [4]. Reflexion operates at a different level of the memory hierarchy: rather than managing raw context, it reinforces language agents through linguistic feedback instead of weight updates, having agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals and store the reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials [5]. The two approaches are thus complementary—MemGPT governs *what context is resident* at any moment [4], whereas Reflexion governs *what lessons persist across trials* [5]—and both illustrate a shift from treating memory as a static prompt to treating it as an actively managed resource.

**Tool use and external API integration.** Toolformer shows that language models can teach themselves to use external tools via simple APIs in a self-supervised way, achieving improved zero-shot performance without sacrificing core language modeling abilities; the model is trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to incorporate results into future token prediction, using self-supervised learning [6]. Notably, whereas ReAct relies on prompting to elicit action generation [2], Toolformer internalizes tool-calling competence through training, representing a distinct methodological choice: scaffolding can be either prompted at inference time or learned during training. This distinction between prompting-based and learning-based approaches recurs across the reviewed literature and complicates direct comparison.

**Retrieval-augmented generation and self-critique.** The retrieval strand has evolved from static, indiscriminate retrieval toward adaptive and self-assessing pipelines. Self-RAG enhances an LM's quality and factuality by learning to retrieve, generate, and critique through self-reflection, addressing the issue that indiscriminate retrieval in RAG can diminish versatility or lead to unhelpful responses; it trains an LM to adaptively retrieve passages on demand and generate self-reflection tokens (retrieval, relevance, support, and utility critiques) to assess and improve its own generation [7]. Corrective RAG (CRAG) improves the robustness of retrieval-augmented generation by assessing retrieval quality and triggering corrective actions, addressing the issue that RAG relies heavily on the relevance of retrieved documents; a lightweight retrieval evaluator assesses the overall quality of retrieved documents and returns a confidence degree that triggers different knowledge retrieval actions, with large-scale web searches [8]. Both approaches thus replace fixed retrieval with quality-aware control—Self-RAG through learned self-reflection tokens [7] and CRAG through an evaluator-triggered correction pipeline [8].

# Comparison of Methods and Approaches

## Overview Table

| Paper | Core Mechanism | Key Innovation | Learning Signal |
|-------|---------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **MemGPT** | OS-inspired hierarchical memory with paging between fast/slow tiers; interrupts for control flow | Virtual context management via memory tiering | Prompting + function calls (no training) |
| **ReAct** | Interleaved reasoning traces + actions in a single prompt | Synergy of reasoning and acting | Few-shot prompting |
| **Toolformer** | Self-supervised API call insertion | Model teaches itself when/how to call tools | Self-supervised (small seed set) |
| **Tree of Thoughts** | Search over tree of "thought" nodes with lookahead/backtracking | Deliberate search over reasoning paths | Prompting + self-evaluation |
| **Self-RAG** | Adaptive retrieval + self-reflection tokens | Learned critique tokens (retrieve/relevant/support/useful) | Supervised fine-tuning on reflection data |
| **Reflexion** | Verbal self-reflection stored in episodic memory | Verbal reinforcement across trials | Trial feedback (no weight updates) |
| **Corrective RAG (CRAG)** | Retrieval evaluator triggers corrective actions (web search, decomposition) | Confidence-based retrieval correction | Lightweight evaluator (trained) |
| **Plan-and-Solve** | Explicit plan-then-execute prompting | Structured zero-shot decomposition | Prompting only |

---

## Key Similarities

**1. Externalizing cognition into structured intermediate steps.**
ReAct (reasoning traces), ToT (thought nodes), Plan-and-Solve (explicit plans), and Reflexion (verbal reflections) all share the premise that making reasoning explicit—rather than implicit in a single forward pass—improves performance. They differ in *granularity*: PS uses a single upfront plan; ReAct interleaves step-by-step; ToT branches into a search tree; Reflexion reflects *after* episodes.

**2. Closing the loop with feedback.**
Self-RAG (self-critique tokens), Reflexion (verbal feedback), CRAG (retrieval confidence), and ToT (self-evaluation of thoughts) all introduce a feedback mechanism where the model assesses its own intermediate output and conditions future behavior on that assessment. The difference is *where* feedback lives: in trained tokens (Self-RAG), in an external memory buffer (Reflexion), in a search controller (ToT), or in a retrieval pipeline (CRAG).

**3. Augmenting the base LLM without full retraining (mostly).**
MemGPT, ReAct, ToT, Reflexion, and Plan-and-Solve are essentially *prompting/orchestration* approaches—they wrap the LLM in a control structure. Toolformer and Self-RAG are the outliers that involve actual training (self-supervised and supervised, respectively). CRAG trains only a lightweight evaluator, not the generator.

**4. Managing limited context.**
MemGPT (memory tiering), Self-RAG (on-demand retrieval), CRAG (selective retrieval correction), and ReAct (compact reasoning traces) all address the context-window bottleneck—but through different levers: architectural paging vs. learned retrieval decisions vs. retrieval quality control vs. compression of thought into traces.

---

## Key Differences

**1. Locus of control: internal vs. external.**
- **Internal (learned in weights):** Toolformer, Self-RAG — the model itself decides when to call tools or retrieve, baked in via training.
- **External (orchestration):** MemGPT, ReAct, ToT, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, CRAG — a scaffold, prompt, or controller governs behavior.
This is the deepest divide: Toolformer/Self-RAG change *what the model is*; the others change *how the model is used*.

**2. Nature of the "memory" or state.**
- MemGPT: hierarchical, paged memory (OS analogy) — persistent, structured.
- Reflexion: episodic buffer of verbal reflections — persistent, unstructured text.
- ToT: transient search tree — discarded after solving.
- ReAct: working context of interleaved traces — transient.
- Self-RAG/CRAG: retrieved passages — external knowledge, not self-state.

**3. Search vs. linear execution.**
ToT is unique in framing problem-solving as *search* (branching, lookahead, backtracking). ReAct, Plan-and-Solve, and Reflexion are essentially linear (or episodic-linear) execution. MemGPT is linear but with memory paging. This makes ToT the most compute-expensive per query and best suited to problems with decomposable search spaces.

**4. Tool/retrieval use.**
- Toolformer: *learned* API invocation (which, when, args).
- Self-RAG: *learned* adaptive retrieval

# Key Strengths and Advantages of the Described Methods

**1. Hierarchical memory management enabling unbounded context (MemGPT).** MemGPT borrows the OS principle of tiered memory—moving data between fast (in-context) and slow (external) storage—so an LLM can maintain coherent, effectively unlimited context across long conversations and documents. The use of interrupts to manage control flow between the system and the model gives fine-grained, event-driven control over when memory operations occur, a capability absent from fixed-context LLMs.

**2. Interleaved reasoning and acting for grounded, adaptive task execution (ReAct).** By generating reasoning traces interleaved with task-specific actions, ReAct lets the model induce, track, and update action plans while handling exceptions as they arise. This synergy between "thinking" and "doing" grounds reasoning in external observations, improving both interpretability and task performance compared to reasoning-only or acting-only baselines.

**3. Self-supervised tool learning without heavy annotation (Toolformer).** Toolformer trains models to decide *which* APIs to call, *when*, *with what arguments*, and *how to incorporate results*—all via self-supervised learning requiring only a handful of demonstrations per API. This makes tool use broadly scalable and cheap to acquire, and it improves future token prediction by integrating real API outputs.

**4. Deliberate search over reasoning paths with self-evaluation (Tree of Thoughts).** ToT frames problem solving as search over a tree of coherent "thought" units, allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate intermediate choices, and look ahead or backtrack. This deliberate, global search substantially outperforms linear chain-of-thought on problems requiring planning and exploration.

**5. Adaptive, self-critiquing retrieval and reflection (Self-RAG, Corrective RAG, Reflexion).** Self-RAG trains the LM to retrieve on demand and emit self-reflection tokens (retrieval, relevance, support, utility) that critique and improve its own generation; Corrective RAG adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator whose confidence score triggers different retrieval actions (including large-scale web search) to correct poor retrievals; Reflexion stores verbal self-reflections in an episodic memory buffer to improve decisions across trials. Together these provide adaptive, self-correcting behavior that reduces hallucination and improves reliability without retraining the base model.

**6. Structured zero-shot planning (Plan-and-Solve).** PS prompting replaces the generic "Let's think step by step" with explicit instructions to understand the problem, extract variables, and devise a plan before executing it—yielding more reliable zero-shot reasoning, with PS+ further refining execution.

# Key Limitations and Weaknesses Across the Papers

**1. Dependence on unreliable self-evaluation and self-critique.**
Several methods rely on the LLM's own judgments to drive control flow, which can be systematically miscalibrated. Self-RAG depends on self-generated reflection tokens (relevance, support, utility) whose reliability is only as good as the model's calibration—errors propagate without external ground truth. Reflexion similarly depends on the agent correctly interpreting task feedback and generating useful verbal reflections; spurious or overgeneralized reflections can reinforce bad strategies across trials. Tree of Thoughts requires the model to self-evaluate partial "thoughts" to prune/search the tree, so search quality collapses when the value heuristic is noisy. Corrective RAG's lightweight retrieval evaluator can misjudge document quality, triggering unnecessary web searches or accepting poor evidence.

**2. Heavy inference-time cost, latency, and engineering complexity.**
MemGPT's OS-inspired memory hierarchy (paging between fast/slow tiers, interrupts) adds substantial orchestration overhead and requires the model to learn complex memory-management function calls, with failure modes around eviction and context overflow. Tree of Thoughts multiplies inference cost through branching, lookahead, and backtracking—often orders of magnitude more calls than chain-of-thought. Self-RAG and Corrective RAG add retrieval and critique passes at every step, increasing latency. Toolformer requires large-scale annotated/self-supervised API-call data and a filtering pipeline, and at inference must detect and execute calls, adding infrastructure burden.

**3. Weak guarantees on when to act, retrieve, or stop.**
Toolformer decides *which* APIs to call and *when* purely from self-supervised likelihood signals, with no explicit reliability or safety check on arguments or outputs—erroneous calls are incorporated into future token prediction. ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions but can loop, hallucinate actions, or fail to recover from exceptions without external scaffolding; its reasoning traces are not guaranteed to be faithful to the actions taken. Plan-and-Solve fixes a plan upfront (understand → extract variables → plan → execute), which is brittle when the initial plan is wrong, since there is limited replanning; PS+ mitigates but does not eliminate this.

**4. Limited generalization beyond the training/benchmark distribution.**
Toolformer's tool-use competence is tied to the APIs and demonstrations seen during self-supervised training, limiting transfer to new tools. Self-RAG and Corrective RAG are tuned to particular retrieval corpora and evaluator behaviors; performance degrades when retrieval quality or domain shifts. Reflexion's episodic memory is task-specific and does not obviously transfer across tasks. MemGPT's memory policies are tuned to particular conversational/document workloads.

**5. Memory and state-management fragility.**
MemGPT's hierarchical memory can lose or corrupt important context through paging/eviction decisions, and the model must learn when to page—an error-prone learned policy. Reflexion's episodic buffer can accumulate stale or contradictory reflections that bias later trials. ReAct has no persistent memory across episodes, so it cannot accumulate experience (unlike Reflexion), while Reflexion cannot easily revise or forget bad lessons.

**6. Evaluation and faithfulness concerns.**
ReAct's and Plan-and-Solve's reasoning traces are post-hoc rationalizations that may not reflect the actual computation, complicating interpretability claims. Tree of Thoughts' gains are demonstrated on narrow puzzle-style tasks (e.g., Game of 24, crosswords) and may not transfer to open-ended problems. Corrective RAG's confidence-threshold actions are heuristic and sensitive to threshold choice, with limited theoretical grounding.

**Most defensible short list (3–5):**
- Self-evaluation unreliability (Self-RAG, Reflexion, ToT, Corrective RAG)
- Inference cost/latency/complexity (MemGPT, ToT, Self-RAG, Toolformer)
- Brittle act/retrieve/stop policies and error propagation (Toolformer, ReAct, Plan-and-Solve)
- Poor out-of-distribution generalization of learned policies (Toolformer, Self-RAG, Reflexion)
- Memory/state fragility and staleness (MemGPT, Reflexion)

section_drafts.content:
The Comparative Analysis section examines how LLM systems enhance capabilities through memory/context management (MemGPT, Reflexion), structured reasoning and planning strategies (ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, Plan-and-Solve), and tool use via external APIs (Toolformer). It further compares retrieval-augmented approaches that incorporate self-critique and self-reflection (Self-RAG, Corrective RAG), highlighting trade-offs in how these methods coordinate memory, reasoning, tooling, and retrieval to improve agent performance.

## Comparative Analysis

The literature on LLM agent reasoning, tool use, and retrieval has developed along several largely parallel tracks: memory and context management [1, 2], reasoning and planning strategies [3, 4, 5], tool use and external API integration [6], and retrieval-augmented generation with self-critique [7, 8]. A comparative reading of these clusters reveals both a clear evolutionary trajectory—from single-pass prompting toward iterative, self-regulating agentic loops—and a set of structural limitations that no individual paper resolves. This section compares the approaches along four dimensions: the mechanism of augmentation, the role of self-evaluation, the treatment of external knowledge and tools, and the computational cost implied by each design.

**From single-pass prompting to iterative deliberation.** Early work in the reasoning cluster treated reasoning as a single forward pass: Plan-and-Solve prompting improves zero-shot chain-of-thought by instructing the model to first devise a plan and then execute sub-tasks, addressing missing-step errors without any external interaction [5]. Tree of Thoughts generalizes this by framing problem solving as search over a tree of coherent "thought" units, allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate intermediate choices, and look ahead or backtrack [4]. ReAct pushes further by interleaving reasoning traces with task-specific actions, so that reasoning helps induce and update action plans while actions interface with external environments [3]. Read together, these three represent a progression in deliberateness—from linear plan execution [5], to branching search [4], to reasoning grounded in environmental feedback [3]—with each step trading additional inference-time computation for greater robustness on multi-step tasks.

**Self-evaluation as a cross-cutting mechanism.** A striking convergence across otherwise distinct clusters is reliance on the model's own judgments to regulate its behavior. In the retrieval cluster, Self-RAG trains the LM to adaptively retrieve passages on demand and to generate self-reflection tokens (retrieval, relevance, support, and utility critiques) that assess and improve its own generation [7], while Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation employs a lightweight retrieval evaluator that returns a confidence degree triggering different corrective retrieval actions, including large-scale web searches [8]. In the memory cluster, Reflexion reinforces agents through linguistic feedback rather than weight updates, storing verbal reflections on task feedback in an episodic memory buffer to improve decisions in subsequent trials [2]. Even Tree of Thoughts embeds self-evaluation as the value function guiding search [4]. This shared dependence on self-critique is notable because none of these papers examines when self-critique fails—systematic blind spots, sycophantic self-evaluation, or error compounding across reflection iterations remain unaddressed across the collection, a critical gap before such loops can be trusted in high-stakes settings.

**Divergent treatments of external knowledge and tools.** The tool-use and retrieval clusters both augment the model with external information but differ fundamentally in mechanism and granularity. Toolformer shows that a model can teach itself, in a self-supervised manner, to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to incorporate results into future token prediction, improving zero-shot performance without sacrificing core language modeling ability [6]. Retrieval methods, by contrast, operate over unstructured documents rather than structured APIs: Self-RAG's contribution is precisely to make retrieval adaptive rather than indiscriminate, since always retrieving can diminish versatility or yield unhelpful responses [7], while CRAG focuses on assessing retrieval quality and triggering corrective actions because RAG relies heavily on document relevance [8]. Notably, the retrieval papers explicitly problematize *when* and *whether* to retrieve [7, 8], whereas Toolformer's learned invocation decisions [6] are evaluated largely in isolation from retrieval or memory concerns—an asymmetry that reflects the absence of any unified architecture jointly managing persistent memory, multi-step planning, and tool invocation. Real-world agentic tasks typically require all three simultaneously, and interactions such as how memory state should inform tool selection, or how tool outputs should be stored and retrieved, remain unstudied.

**Memory as a distinct, and largely disconnected, capability.** The memory cluster addresses a constraint orthogonal to reasoning and retrieval: the finite context window. MemGPT draws inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in operating systems, moving data between fast and slow memory tiers and using interrupts to manage control flow, thereby providing extended context within the LLM's window [1]. Reflexion's episodic memory buffer [2] is complementary but narrower, storing reflective text rather than general context. Neither system is integrated with the planning frameworks of [3, 4, 5] or the retrieval/critique machinery of [7, 8], meaning that claims about memory persistence are not tested in conjunction with deliberate planning or corrective retrieval.

**An evaluation landscape without common ground.** The most consequential comparative observation concerns evaluation. Each method is validated on its own task suite—puzzle-like tasks for Tree of Thoughts [4], API-calling datasets for Toolformer [6], and question-answering sets for Self-RAG and CRAG [7, 8]—so no shared benchmark permits head-to-head comparison across memory, reasoning, retrieval, and tool-use approaches. This fragmentation makes it impossible to determine which technique, or combination, yields the best cost/accuracy trade-off for general agentic workloads. Compounding this, the deliberate-reasoning methods add substantial inference-time computation—branching search in ToT [4], iterative self-reflection in Reflexion [2], and multiple retrieval/critique passes in Self-RAG [7]—yet none of the papers quantifies or optimizes compute and latency cost relative to accuracy gains. The predominance of short, synthetic, or single-turn benchmarks further means that claims about memory persistence [1], iterative self-improvement [2], and planning [5] are not validated under long-horizon, multi-session, realistic deployment conditions. Finally, while retrieval and memory papers focus on whether to retrieve or how to store context [1, 7, 8], none addresses what happens when retrieved documents, stored memories, or tool outputs contradict one another; provenance tracking, confidence weighting, and consistency checking for conflicting information are entirely absent from the collection.

**Summary.** The literature evidences a coherent evolution from static prompting [5] through structured search [4] and interleaved acting [3] to self-regulating retrieval and reflection loops [2, 7, 8], with tool use [6] and hierarchical memory [1] developing as parallel capabilities. The methods are complementary in principle—memory for persistence, planning for structure, retrieval and tools for grounding, and self-critique for quality control—but the collection offers no unified integration of these capabilities, no shared benchmark for cross-method comparison, no cost-aware evaluation of deliberate reasoning, no mechanism for reconciling conflicting information, limited real-world and long-horizon validation, and no analysis of self-critique failure modes. These gaps collectively define the agenda for a comparative, integrative evaluation of agentic LLM systems.

### Method Comparison

# Comparative Analysis

## Overview of the Approaches

The eight papers address distinct but overlapping challenges in LLM capability: **memory management** (MemGPT), **reasoning–action integration** (ReAct), **tool use** (Toolformer), **deliberate search** (Tree of Thoughts), **self-reflective retrieval** (Self-RAG), **verbal reinforcement via reflection** (Reflexion), **retrieval quality control** (Corrective RAG), and **structured zero-shot planning** (Plan-and-Solve). Below, they are compared along key dimensions.

---

## Similarities

**1. Externalizing cognition beyond a single forward pass.**
All methods reject the "one-shot generation" paradigm. MemGPT externalizes memory to a tiered store; ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions; ToT externalizes search over thoughts; Self-RAG and CRAG externalize knowledge retrieval; Reflexion externalizes lessons into an episodic buffer; PS externalizes a plan before execution. The shared premise is that **structure outside the token stream improves reliability**.

**2. Iterative, multi-step control flow.**
ReAct (thought→action→observation loops), Reflexion (trial→feedback→reflection→retry), Self-RAG (retrieve→generate→critique), CRAG (retrieve→evaluate→correct→generate), ToT (expand→evaluate→backtrack), and MemGPT (interrupt-driven control between system and user) all introduce **loops or branching** rather than linear generation. Toolformer and PS are the least iterative: Toolformer bakes decisions into training; PS is a single structured prompt (though PS+ adds verification).

**3. Self-evaluation / self-critique as a mechanism.**
Self-RAG's reflection tokens (relevance, support, utility), Reflexion's verbal self-reflection, ToT's self-evaluation of partial states, and CRAG's confidence-scored retrieval evaluator all instantiate **the model (or a lightweight model) judging its own intermediate outputs** to gate further computation.

**4. Adaptive computation — spend effort only when needed.**
Self-RAG retrieves "on demand"; CRAG triggers different retrieval actions based on confidence; MemGPT pages memory only when needed; ToT expands branches selectively; ReAct calls tools only when reasoning indicates. This contrasts with fixed pipelines (e.g., always-retrieve RAG).

**5. Learning vs. prompting spectrum.**
Toolformer (self-supervised training), Self-RAG (trained reflection tokens), and Reflexion (learning from episodic memory across trials) involve **learning or accumulating experience**. ReAct, ToT, PS, and CRAG are largely **inference-time prompting/architectural wrappers**; MemGPT is a system design with no weight updates.

---

## Differences

**1. Locus of the mechanism.**

| Paper | Where the intelligence lives |
|---|---|
| MemGPT | System architecture (OS-inspired memory tiers, interrupts) |
| ReAct | Prompting (interleaved trace + action format) |
| Toolformer | Model weights (self-supervised API-call training) |
| ToT | Search algorithm over model-generated thoughts |
| Self-RAG | Model weights + inference (trained reflection tokens) |
| Reflexion | Episodic memory buffer + verbal RL loop |
| CRAG | External evaluator module + retrieval pipeline |
| Plan-and-Solve | Prompt template (zero-shot decomposition) |

**2. What is being managed.**
- **Memory/context**: MemGPT (hierarchical tiers, paging), Reflexion (episodic buffer).
- **Knowledge**: Self-RAG, CRAG (retrieval and its correction).
- **Actions/tools**: ReAct, Toolformer.
- **Reasoning paths**: ToT (tree search), PS (plan decomposition), ReAct (trace-guided).
